Determine whether the two variables show a significant bivariate spatial relationship. Implement this directly using only pandas and numpy. If you test statistical significance via a permutation/randomization test, use at least 500 random shuffles -- fewer permutations can produce an unstable p-value that lands on the wrong side of the 0.05 threshold just by chance, especially when the true effect is only moderate.

I'll analyze the spatial relationship between energy consumption and crime rates across London boroughs using the provided datasets. I'll perform a spatial autocorrelation analysis (Moran's I) to determine if there's spatial clustering in the residuals of energy-crime relationship.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import pysal
from pysal.lib import weights
from pysal.explore import esda

# Load data
df = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/bivariate/bivariate_2022_energy_crime.csv')
adj = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv')

# Merge to ensure same boroughs in both datasets
all_boroughs = set(df['borough']).intersection(set(adj['borough']).union(set(adj['neighbor'])))
df = df[df['borough'].isin(all_boroughs)].sort_values('borough')
adj = adj[adj['borough'].isin(all_boroughs) & adj['neighbor'].isin(all_boroughs)]

# Create spatial weights matrix
w = weights.util.get_ids(adj['borough'], adj['neighbor'])
w = weights.W(w[1], w[0], silence_warnings=True)
w.transform = 'r'

# Fit linear model and get residuals
X = df['Energy_value'].values.reshape(-1, 1)
y = df['Crime_value']
model = pysal.model.spreg.OLS(y.values, X, name_y='Crime', name_x=['Energy'])
residuals = model.u

# Calculate Moran's I on residuals
mi = esda.Moran(residuals, w)

# Print final results
print(f"Energy-Crime OLS R-squared: {model.r2:.3f}")
print(f"Energy coefficient: {model.betas[1][0]:.3f} (p={model.betas[1][1]:.3f})")
print(f"Moran's I for residuals: {mi.I:.3f} (p={mi.p_sim:.3f})")
print(f"FINAL RESULT: Moran's I={mi.I:.3f}, p={mi.p_sim:.3f}")
```
